module_title: Maintenance and Repair in Harsh Conditions

lessons.title: Preventive Maintenance Schedules for African Work Conditions
lessons.body: Preventive maintenance is the single most profitable habit you can build into a machinery business in Africa. When a machine breaks down unexpectedly, you lose three times: the repair cost, the lost production, and the customer trust. A planned service costs a fraction of a roadside breakdown. This lesson gives you a practical framework for building maintenance schedules that fit dusty, hot, and remote operating conditions. Start by understanding that manufacturer service intervals are written for controlled environments. In most African sites you face high dust, high ambient temperatures, long haul distances, and fuel and lubricant quality that varies. That means you should shorten intervals, not extend them. A good rule is to cut oil change intervals by 25 to 30 percent and filter changes by up to 50 percent compared to the manual. If the manual says 500 hours, plan for 350 hours. If it says change the air filter when the restriction indicator shows, check it every day in dusty conditions. Build your schedule around four tiers. Daily checks take 15 to 30 minutes before start-up: engine oil level, coolant level, hydraulic oil level, fuel water separator, tyre pressure or track tension, greasing points, and a walk-around for leaks, loose bolts, and cracked hoses. Weekly checks add battery terminals, belt tension, radiator fin cleaning, air filter dust ejection, and brake adjustment. Monthly checks include oil sampling, hydraulic filter inspection, electrical connector cleaning, and torque checks on critical fasteners. Annual or 2000-hour services cover major fluid changes, valve clearance, injector testing, and undercarriage measurement. The key to making this work is a simple paper or phone-based logbook. Every machine gets a card. Every service gets a date, hour meter reading, parts used, and the name of the person who did it. In many African workshops the biggest failure is not lack of skill but lack of records. Without records you cannot prove warranty claims, you cannot predict failures, and you cannot price jobs properly. Assign one person as maintenance controller. This can be the operator on small fleets or a dedicated planner on larger ones. Give them authority to stop a machine that is unsafe or overdue for service. Operators should do daily checks and report anything unusual in writing. A photo on a phone is enough. Train operators to listen for changes in engine note, watch for black smoke, feel for vibration, and smell for overheating or burning. These senses catch problems long before a gauge does. Consumables management is where money is saved or lost. Buy filters in bulk from a reliable supplier and store them in a clean, dry place. Never use compressed air to blow out a paper air filter from the inside; it damages the media. Use genuine or high-quality equivalent parts. Cheap hydraulic filters collapse and send debris through the system, costing ten times the saving. Keep a minimum stock of fast-moving items: engine oil, hydraulic oil, coolant, grease, fuel filters, oil filters, air filters, fan belts, and hose clamps. In remote areas, stock more. Calculate your reorder point based on lead time, not on when you run out. For example, if filters take three weeks to arrive, keep six weeks of stock. Climate matters. In the Sahel and similar hot dry regions, dust destroys air filters and radiator cores. Fit pre-cleaners and clean radiators daily with low-pressure air or water. In humid coastal areas, rust and electrical corrosion are the main enemies. Use dielectric grease on connectors, keep battery terminals clean, and inspect for water ingress after rain. In high-altitude areas, engines lose power and cooling systems work harder; adjust maintenance accordingly. In flood-prone areas, check final drives and axles for water contamination after every wet season. Fuel quality is a major issue across the continent. Water and dirt in diesel destroy injectors and pumps. Always fill from a clean source, use a water separator, and drain it daily. If you store fuel on site, let it settle and draw from above the bottom. Add a biocide if you keep fuel for more than three months. Never use petrol in a diesel engine to save money; the repair bill will be far higher. Lubricants should meet the API or ACEA specification in the manual. If the correct grade is unavailable, use the closest higher specification, not a lower one. Mixing brands is acceptable if specifications match, but mixing different oil types is not. Keep a sample of every oil you use and label it. Oil analysis is cheap insurance. Send samples every 250 to 500 hours to a lab. Results tell you about fuel dilution, coolant leaks, wear metals, and dirt ingress. A single sample is useful; a trend over time is powerful. If silicon rises, you have a dust leak. If iron rises, you have wear. If coolant appears, you have a head gasket or liner problem. Act on the trend before failure. Finally, make maintenance visible. Put a whiteboard in the workshop showing each machine, its next service due, and who is responsible. Review it every Monday. Pay bonuses for zero unplanned breakdowns, not for overtime repairs. That single change in incentives transforms behaviour. A well-run preventive maintenance programme typically cuts breakdowns by 50 to 70 percent, extends machine life by years, and makes your business bankable because you can show lenders and clients that you manage assets professionally.

lessons.title: Diagnosing and Repairing Diesel Engine Faults
lessons.body: Diesel engines power most machinery in Africa, from generators to excavators to trucks. When one fails, the cost of downtime is high, so the ability to diagnose quickly and correctly is a core business skill. This lesson walks through a practical diagnostic sequence, common faults, and repair approaches that work with limited tools and parts. Always start with the basics. A diesel engine needs four things: clean fuel, clean air, compression, and correct timing. If any is missing, it will not run or will run poorly. Before touching anything, ask the operator what happened. Did it lose power gradually or suddenly? Did it smoke? What colour? Did it overheat? Was there a noise? This history narrows the fault faster than any tool. Check the fuel system first because it causes most problems. Start at the tank: is there fuel? Is the tap open? Is the fuel clean? Drain the water separator and look for water or dirt. Check the primary and secondary filters. A clogged filter causes low power and hard starting. Replace, do not clean, paper filters. Check the lift pump; if it is mechanical, hand-prime it and feel for resistance. If electric, listen for the click and check voltage at the terminals. Bleed the system properly. Air in the fuel line is a very common cause of no-start after running out of fuel or changing filters. Bleed from the lowest point to the highest, following the manual sequence. Next check the injection system. On older mechanical engines, check injector timing and spill timing. On common-rail engines, you need a diagnostic scanner to read rail pressure and fault codes. If rail pressure is low, suspect the pressure relief valve, the fuel control actuator, or a worn high-pressure pump. Never open a common-rail line while the engine is cranking; the pressure can cut through skin. Use proper tools and follow safety procedures. If the engine cranks but will not fire, check for white smoke at the exhaust. White smoke with a fuel smell usually means fuel is being injected but not burning, often due to low compression or incorrect timing. Blue smoke means oil burning, often worn rings or valve guides. Black smoke means too much fuel or too little air, often a clogged air filter, a stuck turbo, or a faulty injector. Grey smoke can be timing or injector issues. Compression testing is the next step. On a diesel, compression should be within 10 percent across cylinders and above the minimum in the manual. Low compression on one cylinder points to a valve, piston, or liner problem. Low on all cylinders points to worn rings or a timing issue. A leak-down test tells you where the compression is going: intake valve, exhaust valve, or past the rings. If compression is good, focus on fuel and timing. Overheating is another common fault. Check the coolant level when the engine is cold. Look for leaks at hoses, the water pump, the radiator, and the head gasket. A pressurised cooling system that loses coolant with no visible leak often has a head gasket or cracked head. Use a combustion leak tester to check for exhaust gases in the coolant. Check the thermostat in hot water; it should open at the specified temperature. Check the fan belt and fan clutch. In dusty conditions, clean the radiator core daily. A blocked radiator causes overheating under load even when the coolant is full. If the engine overheats, stop immediately. Continuing to run overheated causes warped heads, scored liners, and seized pistons. Let it cool slowly, then diagnose. Never pour cold water into a hot engine; the block can crack. Knocking or unusual noise needs immediate attention. A deep knock that increases with load often means a big-end or main bearing failure. A sharp knock at half engine speed can be a valve or piston issue. A rattle at the front can be timing gears or a worn damper. Stop the engine and investigate before it destroys itself. Use a stethoscope or a long screwdriver against the block to localise the noise. Oil pressure problems are serious. Low oil pressure can be a worn pump, a stuck relief valve, a clogged pickup screen, or a faulty gauge. Verify with a mechanical gauge before condemning the engine. If pressure is genuinely low, stop running the machine. High oil pressure can be a stuck relief valve or the wrong oil grade. Oil consumption with blue smoke points to worn rings, valve guides, or turbo seals. Check the turbo for play and oil in the intake or exhaust. A failed turbo can send oil into the engine and cause a runaway, where the engine runs on its own oil and cannot be stopped by the key. If that happens, block the air intake immediately with a board or rag, not your hand. Repairs should follow a clear process. Clean the machine before opening it. Use the correct tools; a hammer and chisel on a diesel engine causes expensive damage. Replace gaskets, seals, and stretch bolts as specified. Torque in the correct sequence and to the correct value. Measure, do not guess. Keep parts organised and label connections. Take photos before disassembly. After repair, run the engine at low idle, check for leaks, then load it gradually. Re-torque after the specified hours. In Africa, parts availability is a real constraint. Build relationships with reliable suppliers and keep critical spares: filters, injectors, gaskets, water pumps, thermostats, belts, and sensors. Learn to identify genuine parts versus counterfeits. Counterfeit filters and injectors are common and cause repeat failures. Buy from authorised dealers where possible. Train your team on one engine family at a time. Deep knowledge of a few models is more valuable than shallow knowledge of many. Document every repair with symptoms, tests, findings, parts used, and outcome. That record becomes your most valuable training tool and helps you quote future jobs accurately.

lessons.title: Hydraulic System Maintenance and Troubleshooting
lessons.body: Hydraulic systems power the working parts of most heavy machinery: excavators, loaders, dozers, cranes, and backhoes. When hydraulics fail, the machine stops working even if the engine runs perfectly. This lesson covers how to maintain hydraulic systems in African conditions and how to troubleshoot common faults without expensive guesswork. The first principle is cleanliness. Hydraulic oil is both a power transfer medium and a lubricant. Dirt, water, and metal particles destroy pumps, valves, and cylinders. Most hydraulic failures in Africa are caused by contamination, not by wear alone. Keep everything clean: the oil, the filler cap, the breather, the hoses, and the area around any connection you open. Use a pressure washer carefully around seals; high-pressure water can push dirt into the system. Store oil drums on their sides or under cover, and pump from the top, never from the bottom where water and dirt settle. Check the hydraulic oil level daily with the machine on level ground and the cylinders retracted. Use the correct oil grade as specified. In hot climates, a higher viscosity index oil helps. Do not mix different types of hydraulic oil. If you must top up with a different brand, ensure the specification matches. Keep a sample of the oil you use so you can match it later. Filters are your first line of defence. Replace them at the specified interval, and more often in dusty conditions. A clogged return filter causes high back pressure and can blow seals. A clogged suction filter causes pump cavitation, which sounds like gravel in the pump and destroys it quickly. Never bypass a filter to keep a machine running. That shortcut always costs more. Check the breather on the hydraulic tank. A blocked breather pressurises the tank and causes leaks. Clean or replace it regularly. Check the oil cooler for dirt and fins for damage. Overheated oil loses viscosity and lubricating properties. If the oil is too hot to touch after normal work, investigate: low oil level, blocked cooler, faulty relief valve, or continuous operation against a relief. Water in hydraulic oil turns it milky and causes rust and seal damage. If you see milky oil, drain, flush, and refill. Find the source of water: rain ingress, a cracked cooler, or a washed machine. Troubleshooting starts with symptoms. Slow operation in all functions usually means low pump output, low relief pressure, or a clogged suction strainer. Slow operation in one function points to that circuit: a worn cylinder, a faulty valve, or a collapsed hose. No movement in one function can be a broken linkage, a stuck spool, or a failed solenoid. Excessive heat can be a relief valve stuck open, wrong oil, or a restricted return line. Noise from the pump often means cavitation from low oil, a clogged suction filter, or air in the system. Whining that changes with load can be a worn pump. A knocking sound can be a loose drive coupling. Check the simple things first. Is the oil level correct? Is the suction strainer clean? Is the breather clear? Is the correct oil in the tank? Is the pump drive engaged? Is the emergency stop or safety lever in the right position? Many call-outs end with a simple fix that was overlooked. Pressure testing is the next step. Use a calibrated gauge and the test ports provided. Compare readings to the manual. Low main relief pressure causes weak operation across all functions. Adjust only if the manual allows and only with a gauge connected. Do not turn relief valves blindly; you can damage the pump or the valve. Flow testing tells you if the pump is worn. A flow meter is expensive, but a good workshop can test pump flow and compare to specification. If flow is low at rated pressure, the pump is worn and should be rebuilt or replaced. Cylinder problems show as drift, slow movement, or external leaks. Drift means the piston seal is bypassing. External leaks mean the rod seal or wiper is worn. A bent rod causes seal failure and must be straightened or replaced. When repairing a cylinder, work in a clean area, use the correct seal kit, and protect the rod from damage. Torque the gland correctly and bleed the air after reassembly. Hoses and fittings fail from age, heat, abrasion, and pressure spikes. Inspect hoses regularly for cracks, blisters, and rubbing. Replace, do not repair, a damaged hose. Use the correct pressure rating and compatible fittings. When making a hose, ensure the crimp is correct and the hose is clean inside. A dirty hose contaminates the system. In remote areas, carry a hose repair kit and a selection of fittings. But remember that a field repair is temporary; replace with a proper hose as soon as possible. Contamination control is a daily discipline. Use filter carts to clean oil during changes. Keep a supply of clean containers. Never use a dirty bucket to catch hydraulic oil. Cover open ports with clean caps or plastic. Train everyone to treat hydraulic oil like medicine: clean, sealed, and labelled. Oil analysis every 500 hours tells you about wear metals, water, and viscosity. A rising iron or copper level points to pump or motor wear. Silicon means dirt ingress. Water means a leak or condensation. Act on the trend. Finally, document everything. Keep a log of pressures, temperatures, oil changes, and repairs. When a machine has a recurring fault, the log shows the pattern. That pattern is your path to a permanent fix. A well-maintained hydraulic system can last 10,000 hours or more. A neglected one fails in a fraction of that time. The difference is discipline, not luck.

lessons.title: Undercarriage and Tyre Care for Harsh Terrain
lessons.body: Undercarriage and tyres are among the highest cost items in machinery ownership, often 30 to 50 percent of total operating cost. In Africa, terrain ranges from soft sand to sharp rock, from mud to laterite, and from smooth tarmac to broken bush tracks. This lesson shows how to inspect, maintain, and repair undercarriage and tyres to get maximum life and minimum downtime. Start with daily inspection. For tracked machines, walk around and look at the tracks. Check for loose or missing shoes, worn bushings, leaking rollers, and damaged sprockets. Measure track tension according to the manual. Too tight causes wear on bushings and sprockets; too loose causes derailment and damaged links. In sandy conditions, tension should be on the loose side; in rocky conditions, slightly tighter. Check the idler and recoil spring for cracks and leaks. Look for oil leaking from rollers and idlers, which means a failed seal. A dry roller will seize and damage the track. Grease the track adjuster as specified. For wheeled machines, check tyre pressure daily when tyres are cold. Correct pressure extends tyre life, improves fuel economy, and prevents overheating. Under-inflation causes sidewall flex, heat, and blowouts. Over-inflation causes uneven wear and impact damage. Use a calibrated gauge, not a kick. Check for cuts, embedded stones, and bulges. Remove stones from treads before they work deeper. Check wheel nuts for tightness and look for oil leaks from hubs. Tyre selection matters. For haul trucks on sharp rock, use cut-resistant compounds and deep treads. For loaders in sand, use wide tyres at low pressure for flotation. For graders, use the correct tread pattern for the job. Bias tyres are cheaper and tougher for slow work; radial tyres give better fuel economy and longer life on long hauls. Match the tyre to the job, not just to the rim. In many African operations, mixing tyre types on the same axle causes handling problems and uneven wear. Keep the same size, type, and tread depth across an axle. Rotate tyres as recommended to even out wear. Keep a tyre log: serial number, position, hours, pressure checks, and repairs. That log tells you which positions wear fastest and helps you plan replacements. Track wear is measured in three ways: link height, bushing diameter, and sprocket wear. Use a wear gauge or a caliper. Record measurements every 250 hours. When wear reaches the limit, plan replacement before failure. A worn sprocket accelerates bushing wear, so replace sprockets and chains together when possible. Turn pins and bushings if the design allows; this doubles life for a fraction of the cost of new tracks. Rollers and idlers should turn freely and not leak. A seized roller will flat-spot and damage the link. Replace in sets where possible to keep wear even. Track shoes wear on the grouser height. Measure and replace when below the limit. In abrasive conditions, use shoes with more wear material. In soft ground, use wider shoes for flotation. Undercarriage life is also about operation. Train operators to avoid spinning tracks, turning on hard surfaces, and running over large rocks. Smooth operation saves undercarriage more than any maintenance. For tyres, train operators to avoid kerbs, sharp rocks, and overheating. On long hauls, stop and check tyre temperature; hot tyres are a warning. Do not reduce pressure on hot tyres; wait for them to cool. Repairing tyres in the field is possible for small punctures with plugs, but sidewall damage and large cuts need a proper vulcanised repair. Keep a spare wheel and tyre for critical machines. In remote areas, carry a tyre repair kit, a good jack, and a torque wrench. Never work under a machine supported only by a jack; use stands. Wheel nut torque is critical. Loose nuts cause wheel loss and accidents. Tighten in a star pattern to the specified torque. Re-torque after 50 to 100 hours on new or repaired wheels. Use a torque wrench, not a breaker bar and guesswork. Undercarriage and tyre costs are predictable if you measure. Build a replacement forecast based on hours and wear rates. Budget for it monthly. That way, when replacement is due, you have the money and you are not forced into a cheap, short-life option. A machine that is down waiting for tyres loses more money than the tyres cost. Finally, keep records and use them. Compare wear rates between machines and operators. If one machine wears out tracks twice as fast, find out why. It may be terrain, but it may also be operation or maintenance. Fix the cause, not just the symptom. Good undercarriage and tyre management is one of the clearest ways to turn a machinery business from a constant cash drain into a profitable, predictable operation.

lessons.title: Workshop Safety, Tools, and Cost Control
lessons.body: A safe workshop is a productive workshop. In Africa, many machinery businesses operate with limited space, limited tools, and high pressure to get machines back to work. That pressure causes accidents and costly mistakes. This lesson covers safety, tool management, and cost control so you can run a professional workshop that protects people and profits. Start with safety rules that everyone follows, including the owner. Wear correct personal protective equipment: safety boots, overalls, gloves, eye protection, and hearing protection when using grinders or hammers. Never wear loose clothing or jewellery around rotating parts. Tie back long hair. Use the right tool for the job; a chisel is not a spanner. Keep the workshop clean and dry. Oil and water on the floor cause falls. Store parts and tools off the floor. Keep walkways clear. Use drip trays under machines. Clean up spills immediately with sand or absorbent material. Fire safety is critical. Store fuel, oil, and gas cylinders away from welding and grinding. Keep fire extinguishers serviced and accessible. Train everyone to use them. Have a first aid kit and a person trained in first aid. Know the emergency numbers and the route to the nearest clinic. Lifting is a major cause of injury. Use jacks, stands, cranes, or hoists rated for the load. Never work under a machine supported only by a jack. Use axle stands or blocks. When lifting with a crane, use certified slings and check them before use. Keep people out of the lift zone. Use a signal person if the operator cannot see the load. Electrical safety matters. Use proper plugs, cables, and earth leakage protection. Do not run cables through water. Repair damaged cables immediately. Lock out and tag out before working on electrical systems or any stored energy. This includes hydraulic pressure, compressed air, and springs. Bleed pressure before opening lines. Support raised components with mechanical stops, not hydraulics. Hand tools should be inspected regularly. A mushroomed chisel or a cracked hammer handle can cause serious injury. Replace damaged tools. Keep cutting tools sharp; a blunt tool needs more force and slips. Store tools in a shadow board or labelled drawers so you can see what is missing. Power tools need correct guards and regular checks. Use the right blade or disc for the material. Never remove a guard to save time. Welding requires a screen, gloves, and ventilation. Never weld near fuel or paint. Check the area for flammable material before striking an arc. Tool management is also a cost issue. Tools disappear, get damaged, or are borrowed and not returned. Assign a tool controller. Use a sign-out sheet for special tools. Keep a minimum stock of consumables: drill bits, grinding discs, welding rods, bolts, and sealants. Buy quality tools; cheap tools break and cause injuries and poor work. But do not buy a tool you use once a year if you can hire it. Cost control starts with knowing your costs. Separate direct costs (parts, labour, consumables for a specific job) from indirect costs (rent, electricity, tools, administration). Know your hourly rate. Calculate it by adding all annual costs and dividing by billable hours. Most workshops undercharge because they forget indirect costs. Quote jobs using a standard format: diagnosis, parts, labour, consumables, and contingency. Get approval before starting. Document everything. A job card should record the machine, hours, complaint, diagnosis, work done, parts used, labour hours, and the person who did the work. This protects you in disputes and helps you price future jobs. Parts management is where many businesses lose money. Keep fast-moving parts in stock, but do not tie up cash in slow movers. Use a simple bin card or spreadsheet. Record every part in and out. Do a stock count monthly. Watch for theft and waste. Buy in bulk where it saves money, but only for items you use regularly. Build relationships with suppliers. Ask for trade prices, credit terms, and technical support. Pay on time to keep credit. In remote areas, keep a larger stock of critical parts because lead times are long. Labour productivity matters. Plan the day the evening before. Have parts and tools ready before the job starts. Avoid waiting time. Train your team continuously. A skilled technician fixes it right the first time. An unskilled one creates repeat failures. Pay fairly and on time. A stable team is cheaper than constant recruitment. Finally, review your numbers monthly. Look at revenue, costs, profit, and the top five jobs by value. Identify where you lost money and fix it. A workshop that measures its costs and its safety will outperform one that runs on guesswork. Safety and profit are not opposites; they are the same discipline applied to different risks. Protect your people, protect your tools, and protect your cash, and your machinery business will grow.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Machinery Maintenance Data, Tolerances, and Field Decision Tables for African Conditions

This practical reference consolidates the numbers, tolerances, and decision rules that workshop teams across sub-Saharan Africa need when maintaining tractors, power tillers, combine harvesters, and diesel irrigation pumps. It is written for the manager who must decide whether to repair, replace, or run to failure â decisions that directly affect cost per hectare, harvest timing, and downtime risk during short planting windows. Use it alongside the earlier lessons on preventive schedules, diesel diagnostics, hydraulics, undercarriage care, and workshop safety.

The guiding principle is business-first: every maintenance action should be justified by avoided downtime, extended asset life, or reduced fuel and repair cost. In African conditions, the dominant failure drivers are abrasive dust, high ambient temperatures, variable fuel quality, long supply chains for spare parts, and operator skill gaps. The tables below convert those realities into actionable reference data.

Table 1: Service and Replacement Intervals for African Operating Conditions

Manufacturer intervals assume clean fuel, low dust, and moderate temperatures. In African field conditions â particularly dry-season tillage, harrowing, and threshing â intervals should be shortened. The figures below are field-adapted recommendations drawn from FAO and manufacturer guidance.

Component / Consumable Standard Interval African Field Interval Typical Cost Driver Failure Consequence
Engine oil & filter 250 hours 150â200 hours Oil, filter, labour Bearing seizure, engine rebuild
Primary air filter 500 hours 100â250 hours Filter element Bore polishing, power loss
Fuel filter / water separator 500 hours 250â300 hours Filter, drain time Injector and pump damage
Hydraulic oil & filter 1,000 hours 600â800 hours Oil, filter, seals Valve scoring, lift failure
Transmission oil 1,000 hours 800â1,000 hours Oil, labour Gear and clutch wear
Coolant 2,000 hours / 2 years 1,000 hours / 1 year Coolant, flush Overheating, liner cavitation
Greasing (all nipples) 50 hours 10â25 hours (daily in dust) Grease, labour Pin, bush, and bearing failure
Battery terminals / electrolyte 250 hours Monthly Clean, distilled water No-start, alternator strain

Sources: FAO Agricultural Engineering in Development: Farm Power and Machinery; manufacturer service manuals (John Deere, Massey Ferguson, Kubota) as adapted for dusty and high-temperature African operating conditions. Hours are engine-hour-meter readings unless stated.

Table 2: Field Diagnostic Decision Matrix â Symptom to Action

This matrix helps a workshop manager or lead mechanic decide whether to continue operating, service immediately, or stop and repair. It reflects the reality that in remote African locations, a wrong "run it" decision can destroy an engine, while an unnecessary "stop" decision can lose a planting window.

Symptom Likely Cause Immediate Action Risk if Ignored Est. Cost Band (USD)
Black exhaust smoke under load Clogged air filter, over-fuelling Clean/replace air filter; check injectors Power loss, bore wear 10â80
White smoke, hard starting Water in fuel, injector fault, low compression Drain water separator; test injectors Injector pump failure 50â600
Blue smoke, oil consumption Worn rings, valve guides, turbo seal Compression test; plan overhaul Catastrophic engine failure 400â3,000
Hydraulic lift slow or jerky Low oil, clogged filter, worn pump Check level and filter; pressure test Pump and valve damage 30â1,200
Overheating in field Dust-blocked radiator, low coolant, thermostat Stop; clean radiator; check coolant Cracked head, seized engine 20â2,500
Excessive tyre wear on one side Misalignment, incorrect pressure, worn linkage Check pressure and alignment Premature tyre replacement 100â800
Fuel consumption rising >15% Injectors, air filter, dragging brakes Full service; flow-test injectors High operating cost, engine damage 20â500
Unusual metallic noise Bearing, gear, or valve train failure Stop immediately; diagnose Total component destruction 200â5,000

Cost bands are indicative 2024â2025 estimates for sub-Saharan African workshops and will vary by country, import duty, and parts availability. Sources: FAO farm machinery maintenance guidance; ILRI mechanisation and smallholder equipment reports; manufacturer diagnostic manuals.

⚠ SAFETY WARNING â CHEMICALS, FUELS, AND EXHAUST: Diesel fuel, engine oil, hydraulic fluid, coolant, and battery electrolyte are hazardous. Diesel and exhaust fumes contain substances classified as carcinogenic; never run engines in enclosed sheds or near workers. Battery electrolyte contains sulphuric acid and can cause severe burns and blindness â always wear acid-resistant gloves and eye protection when handling batteries. Used oil can cause skin cancer with repeated exposure; wash thoroughly and never use bare hands. Coolant (ethylene glycol) is toxic if swallowed and attractive to children and animals â store in sealed, labelled containers. In many African markets, fuel and lubricants may be adulterated or contaminated; filter and settle fuel before use, and never siphon by mouth. Dispose of used oil, filters, and coolant through approved collection points, not on soil or in waterways.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Daily (pre-start): Check engine oil, coolant, hydraulic oil, and fuel level; drain water separator; inspect for leaks and loose bolts; clean radiator screen and air pre-cleaner.
  • Every 10â25 hours in dust: Grease all nipples; check tyre pressures and wheel nut torque; clean air filter housing; inspect belts and hoses.
  • Every 150â200 hours: Change engine oil and filter; replace or clean primary air filter; inspect fuel filter and replace if restricted.
  • Every 250â300 hours: Replace fuel filters; check injector performance; inspect battery terminals and electrolyte level.
  • Every 600â800 hours: Change hydraulic oil and filter; inspect hydraulic hoses and couplings; test lift and pressure.
  • Seasonally: Full coolant flush; transmission oil change; undercarriage and tyre inspection; brake and steering adjustment.
  • Before each season: Stock critical spares (filters, belts, hoses, injector washers, grease, coolant) to avoid downtime during planting and harvest.
  • Record-keeping: Log every service hour, part number, cost, and fault in a workshop register â this data drives repair-versus-replace decisions and proves asset value to lenders and insurers.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Sustainable Agricultural Mechanisation: guidance on machinery selection, maintenance, and policy for developing countries.
  • FAO â Farm Power and Machinery (Agricultural Engineering in Development): classic reference on tractor and implement maintenance.
  • ILRI â Mechanisation and Smallholder Farming: research on appropriate equipment and service models in East and West Africa.
  • WHO â Guidelines for the Safe Use of Wastewater, Excreta and Greywater (relevant to chemical and fuel handling safety): occupational and environmental safety reference.
  • Michigan State University Extension â Farm Machinery and Safety Resources: practical extension bulletins on tractor safety, maintenance, and diesel engine care.

Use this reference as a workshop wall document. The intervals and decision rules are starting points â adjust them to your soil type, dust load, fuel quality, and machine age. The business case is simple: a tractor that is serviced on schedule costs less per hectare, lasts longer, and fails less often during the weeks when failure is most expensive. In African agribusiness, maintenance discipline is not a cost centre â it is a profit centre.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a lockout tagout procedure before repairing machinery?
options: B) To prevent accidental energization during maintenance
D) To test the machine under load
quiz.explanation: Lockout tagout isolates energy sources so the machine cannot start or release stored energy while a technician is working on it.

quiz.q: Which document should always be consulted before performing a repair on unfamiliar equipment?
quiz.explanation: The manufacturer service manual provides correct specifications, torque values, and safe repair procedures for the specific machine.

quiz.q: What does excessive vibration in a rotating machine most commonly indicate?
quiz.explanation: Vibration is often caused by misaligned shafts, unbalanced rotating parts, or worn bearings that need correction.

quiz.q: Why should hydraulic system pressure be relieved before disconnecting any lines?
options: A) To prevent injury from pressurized fluid
quiz.explanation: Trapped hydraulic pressure can cause sudden fluid release, injection injuries, or uncontrolled movement of components.

quiz.q: What is the correct action when a machine guard is removed for repair?
options: A) Leave it off if production is urgent
B) Replace it before returning the machine to service
C) Store it in the parts room permanently
D) Tape over the safety switch
quiz.explanation: Guards must be reinstalled and verified before the machine is returned to operation to protect operators from hazards.

quiz.q: Which type of maintenance is performed based on measured condition rather than a fixed schedule?
quiz.explanation: Predictive maintenance uses condition monitoring data to schedule repairs only when indicators show it is needed.

quiz.q: What should be done with used oil and filters after a machine service?
options: A) Pour them down a drain
B) Store them with clean supplies
C) Dispose of them according to environmental regulations
D) Burn them in an open area
quiz.explanation: Used oil and filters are regulated waste and must be handled, stored, and disposed of through approved environmental procedures.

quiz.q: What is the best way to verify a repair was successful before full production resumes?
options: A) Assume it works if it starts
C) Skip the test run to save time
D) Perform a controlled test run and inspect readings
quiz.explanation: A controlled test run allows the technician to check temperature, pressure, vibration, and function before full operation.

quiz.q: Why should preventive maintenance intervals be shortened in dusty African work conditions?
options: A) Dust accelerates filter clogging and wear
quiz.explanation: Dust accelerates filter clogging and component wear so service intervals must be shortened.

quiz.q: Which factor most affects maintenance scheduling in hot African climates?
options: B) High ambient temperatures and heat stress on fluids
quiz.explanation: High ambient temperatures degrade oils and coolants faster, requiring adjusted schedules.

quiz.q: What is the best first step when a diesel engine cranks but will not start?
options: B) Check fuel supply and air intake
quiz.explanation: Fuel and air supply are the most common causes and should be checked first.

quiz.q: Black smoke from a diesel exhaust usually indicates what?
options: B) Incomplete combustion from rich fuel or restricted air
quiz.explanation: Black smoke indicates incomplete combustion often from excess fuel or restricted air.

quiz.q: White smoke from a cold diesel engine that persists after warm-up may indicate what?
options: A) Water in fuel or coolant entering cylinders
quiz.explanation: Persistent white smoke suggests water in fuel or coolant entering the combustion chamber.

quiz.q: Which hydraulic symptom most likely indicates a clogged suction strainer?
options: B) Pump cavitation and noisy operation
quiz.explanation: A clogged suction strainer causes cavitation and noisy pump operation.

quiz.q: What is the correct action when hydraulic oil appears milky?
options: B) Drain, flush, and find the water source
C) Ignore it until next year
D) Add more hydraulic oil only
quiz.explanation: Milky oil indicates water contamination requiring drain, flush, and source repair.

quiz.q: Hydraulic hoses should be replaced when they show what?
options: B) Cracks, bulges, or weeping fittings
quiz.explanation: Cracks, bulges, and weeping fittings are signs a hose must be replaced.

quiz.q: Why is undercarriage maintenance critical on African earthmoving machines?
options: A) It is the cheapest part
B) It is expensive and wears fast in abrasive terrain
quiz.explanation: Undercarriage is costly and wears rapidly in abrasive African terrain.

quiz.q: What is the recommended track tension check method?
options: B) Measure sag per manufacturer specification
quiz.explanation: Track sag must be measured against the manufacturer specification.

quiz.q: Why should tyre pressure be checked when tyres are cold?
options: A) Hot tyres give false high readings
quiz.explanation: Hot tyres give false high pressure readings so cold checks are accurate.

quiz.q: Which tyre damage is common on harsh African terrain?
quiz.explanation: Sharp rocks and debris cause sidewall cuts and punctures on harsh terrain.

quiz.q: What should be done before working under a raised machine?
options: A) Rely on the hydraulic jack only
B) Use certified stands and chock wheels
C) Ask a colleague to hold it
quiz.explanation: Certified stands and wheel chocks are required before working under a raised machine.

quiz.q: Which PPE is essential when grinding metal in the workshop?
quiz.explanation: Face shield and goggles protect eyes and face from grinding sparks and debris.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of keeping a workshop tool inventory?
options: A) Reduces theft and loss and controls costs
quiz.explanation: Tool inventory reduces theft, loss, and unnecessary purchases, controlling costs.

quiz.q: How can cost control be improved in a busy African workshop?
options: B) Track parts usage and repair versus replace decisions
quiz.explanation: Tracking parts usage and repair versus replace decisions improves cost control.

quiz.q: What does a daily walk-around inspection help detect?
options: B) Leaks, loose parts, and tyre damage before failure
quiz.explanation: Walk-around inspections detect leaks, loose parts, and tyre damage early.

quiz.q: Which coolant type is generally preferred for hot African diesel engines?
options: B) Correctly mixed ethylene glycol or manufacturer coolant
quiz.explanation: Correctly mixed coolant protects against overheating and corrosion in hot climates.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a fuel-water separator on diesel machines?
options: B) Remove water and contaminants from fuel
quiz.explanation: Fuel-water separators remove water and contaminants that damage injection systems.

quiz.q: When should hydraulic filters be replaced?
options: A) Only when the machine stops
B) At manufacturer intervals or when indicators show restriction
quiz.explanation: Hydraulic filters must be replaced at specified intervals or when restriction is indicated.

quiz.q: What is a safe practice when refuelling a diesel machine?
options: B) Shut off engine and use bonding if required
C) Use a phone while refuelling
quiz.explanation: Shutting off the engine and following bonding rules prevents fire and explosion risks.

quiz.q: Which record best supports preventive maintenance planning?
options: A) Machine hour meter and service log
quiz.explanation: Machine hour meter and service logs are essential for planning maintenance intervals.
